ann_36.text: This part acts on 117 of 242 training patients (48%), and 77 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with a flat ST segment, 1.6 mm of ST depression and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 88% to about 92% (on the training data only).

Through it, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 19% to about 28%, and it adds risk only once ST depression rises above about 0.9 mm (on the training data only).
More ST depression clearly raises the predicted risk even more if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect (from about 35% to about 84%, against about 19% to about 48% otherwise).

Both more ST depression and a reversible thallium defect clearly raise it more if the resting ECG is normal (from about 19% to about 48% and to about 44%, against about 26% to about 37% and to about 43% otherwise).
On its own through this part, a reversible thallium defect and the resting ECG change the predicted risk only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_38.text: This part barely changes the predictions.

Through it, a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers the predicted risk only slightly for the typical patient it acts on (a 56-year-old man with a flat ST segment, 1.4 mm of ST depression and a reversible defect on the thallium scan, predicted risk about 89%); the model has little data on this (15 patients), on the training data only.

ann_39.text: This part acts on 203 of 242 training patients (84%), and 102 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, a flat ST segment and 1.0 mm of ST depression), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 61% to about 63% (on the training data only).

Through it, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 19% to about 36%, and it adds risk only once ST depression rises above about 1.3 mm (on the training data only).

This rise from ST depression is clearly larger if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect (from about 35% to about 84%) than if it shows neither a fixed nor a reversible defect (from about 19% to about 48%).
It is slightly larger if resting blood pressure is at or below 130 mm Hg (from about 16% to about 45%, against about 25% to about 52% above 130 mm Hg; on the training data only).
A reversible thallium defect, older age, chest pain type and the resting ECG change the predicted risk only slightly through this part (on the training data only).

ann_40.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 2%), non-anginal chest pain (about 4%) or atypical angina (about 11%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 19%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 19% to about 88%, a flat ST segment raises it to about 59%, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) to about 48%, and a reversible thallium defect to about 44% (on the training data only).

Higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) raises it from about 13% to about 34%, higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) from about 13% to about 32%, chest pain brought on by exercise from about 19% to about 30%, and older age (42 to 66 years) from about 16% to about 23% (on the training data only).

Being a woman lowers it from about 19% to about 2%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 10%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute from about 26% to about 16% (on the training data only).

A fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 10% (15 patients), and a thallium result coded 4 raises it to about 36% (2 patients); the model has little data on this, and both hold on the training data only.
A downsloping rather than upsloping ST segment raises it only slightly, to about 22% (17 patients; the model has little data on this; on the training data only).

ann_36.original: Hidden gate 204 = ReLU(2.554*oldpeak + 1.133*thal:7 + 0.937*restecg:0 + 0.276): a one-sided ischaemia-evidence detector that switches on for patients with exercise-induced ST depression and/or a reversible thallium defect, normal resting ECG adding a little. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): hard-zero for 52%, active for 48%; mean |grad| oldpeak 1.23 > thal:7 0.55 > restecg:0 0.45; oldpeak alone correlates 0.88 with the gate. This is the output-facing copy 204_a (bit-identical to 204_b); it reads out directly to the output with +0.117, raising predicted risk.
ann_36.proposed: A part that acts on about half the patients; through it, ST depression above about 0.9 mm raises the predicted risk, more so with a reversible thallium defect or a normal resting ECG.

ann_38.original: Serial chain thal:6 -> 3671 -> 2116: 3671 = ReLU(1.000*thal:6 + 2.123), 2116 = ReLU(1.003*3671 + 0.036). Since thal:6 >= -0.257 on the data both ReLUs are always active (100% on train), so 2116 = 1.003*thal:6 + 2.165 exactly (r = 1.000 on train). It feeds gate 290 with weight -0.013, contributing -0.013*thal:6 - 0.029 to its pre-activation: an always-on affine relay that is functionally a vestige.
ann_38.proposed: A part that barely changes the predictions; a fixed thallium defect lowers the risk only slightly through it.

ann_39.original: Serial composition of the ischaemia gate into a BP-adjusted gate and its readouts. (1) Gate 290 = ReLU(1.088*st_ischaemia_gate_bp - 0.817*trestbps + 0.151*cp:2 + 0.017*cp:3 + 0.046*thal:6 - 0.013*thal6_linear_passthrough - 0.485): it passes on the ischaemia evidence of 204_b, offset downward by resting blood pressure (high-BP patients need more ST-depression evidence to open it). (2) 1834 = ReLU(0.941*290 - 1.672): high-threshold amplifier, fires only when 290 > 1.78, making the pathway convex. (3) 1987 = ReLU(0.880*age - 1.585*290 + 0.179): an age term switched OFF by the gate, so age adds risk only for patients in whom 290 is quiet. Output contribution 0.135*290 + 0.165*1834 + 0.097*1987. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 290 active 56% (100/135 of its active cases have 204 on; 35 open from low BP alone, mean predicted risk 0.13); 1834 active 26%, only when 204 and 290 are both on, and 78% of those patients are diseased; 1987 active in 64% of patients with 290 quiet vs 13% with 290 active. The thal:6 chain is functionally inert. Interpretation: the network has exactly one nonlinear mechanism - an ischaemia pathway that amplifies strong ST-depression/defect evidence and uses age as a fallback signal when that evidence is absent.
ann_39.proposed: A part that acts on most patients; through it, ST depression above about 1.3 mm raises the predicted risk, more so with a reversible thallium defect.

ann_40.original: Root: logit z = -0.496 + LINEAR CORE + 0.117*st_ischaemia_gate_output + ischaemia_pathway readouts (0.135*290 + 0.165*1834 + 0.097*1987); prediction = sigmoid(z) (the genome output node is ReLU but the evaluator overrides it with sigmoid for binary classification, so it is a logistic score). LINEAR CORE (18 direct input->output edges, z-scored inputs): ca +1.51, sex:0 -1.08, slope:1 -0.90, chol +0.53, cp:1 -0.53, trestbps +0.49, cp:3 -0.47, thal:3 -0.43, exang:1 +0.43, slope:3 -0.41, thal:6 -0.38, cp:4 +0.33, fbs:0 +0.28, thalach -0.25, restecg:0 -0.18, exang:0 +0.15, age +0.11, thal:7 -0.07. Signs match cardiology: more fluoroscopy-coloured vessels, male sex, high cholesterol/BP, exertional angina and asymptomatic chest pain raise risk; upsloping ST (slope:1), normal thallium (thal:3), typical/non-anginal pain and high max heart rate lower it. 6 inputs are unused (sex:1, fbs:1, restecg:1, restecg:2, slope:2, thal:4 - mostly redundant one-hot complements or rare categories). COMPOSITION: purely additive in the logit - the two children add to the linear core. Child 1 (st_ischaemia_gate_output) adds a ReLU ischaemia score (oldpeak, thal:7, restecg:0); child 2 (ischaemia_pathway) adds a BP-adjusted, convexly amplified version of the same score, plus an age term that is active only when the score is quiet. oldpeak and thal:7 influence the output ONLY through these gates (oldpeak has no direct edge). EVIDENCE (train, n=242): full model AUC 0.942 / acc 0.876; linear core alone AUC 0.932 (nonlinear parts add +0.010 train AUC); logit SD of linear core 3.18 vs 0.78 for all nonlinear readouts combined. Removing individual readouts: 290 -0.002, 1834 -0.0016, 204_a -0.0016, 1987 -0.0007, whole pathway -0.0055 AUC. Whole-model SHAP (prob scale): ca 0.139, sex:0 0.105, slope:1 0.099, thal:3 0.045, cp:3 0.041, exang:1 0.039, oldpeak 0.038, chol 0.033, cp:4 0.032. The model is essentially a logistic regression with one small nonlinear ischaemia correction.
ann_40.proposed: Typical angina, non-anginal chest pain and atypical angina lower the predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms. More vessels coloured, a flat ST segment, more ST depression, a reversible thallium defect, higher cholesterol, higher resting blood pressure, chest pain on exercise and older age raise it; being a woman, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL and a higher maximum heart rate lower it.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk about 19%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 2%), non-anginal chest pain (about 4%) or atypical angina (about 11%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 19% to about 88%, and a flat rather than upsloping ST segment at peak exercise raises it to about 59% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise raises the predicted risk, and even more so if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect: going from 0 to 2.8 mm clearly moves it from about 35% to about 84% with that defect, against about 19% to about 48% without it.

A reversible defect on the thallium scan raises the predicted risk, and even more so if the resting ECG is normal: for a typical patient it clearly moves from about 19% to about 44% with a normal resting ECG, and from about 26% to about 43% otherwise.
Being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 19% to about 2% (on the training data only).
One small part barely changes the predictions.

parts.original_hypothesis: Serial composition of the ischaemia gate into a BP-adjusted gate and its readouts. (1) Gate 290 = ReLU(1.088*st_ischaemia_gate_bp - 0.817*trestbps + 0.151*cp:2 + 0.017*cp:3 + 0.046*thal:6 - 0.013*thal6_linear_passthrough - 0.485): it passes on the ischaemia evidence of 204_b, offset downward by resting blood pressure (high-BP patients need more ST-depression evidence to open it). (2) 1834 = ReLU(0.941*290 - 1.672): high-threshold amplifier, fires only when 290 > 1.78, making the pathway convex. (3) 1987 = ReLU(0.880*age - 1.585*290 + 0.179): an age term switched OFF by the gate, so age adds risk only for patients in whom 290 is quiet. Output contribution 0.135*290 + 0.165*1834 + 0.097*1987. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 290 active 56% (100/135 of its active cases have 204 on; 35 open from low BP alone, mean predicted risk 0.13); 1834 active 26%, only when 204 and 290 are both on, and 78% of those patients are diseased; 1987 active in 64% of patients with 290 quiet vs 13% with 290 active. The thal:6 chain is functionally inert. Interpretation: the network has exactly one nonlinear mechanism - an ischaemia pathway that amplifies strong ST-depression/defect evidence and uses age as a fallback signal when that evidence is absent.
